claims.claim: Leandro Andrade stole nine children's videotapes in two K-Mart thefts (Ontario and Montclair, California) in November 1995.
claims.episode_span: a fifty-to-life term for Leandro Andrade after he shoplifted nine videotapes from two Kmart stores in Ontario, California
claims.supporting_quote: On November 4, 1995, Leandro Andrade, a nine-year Army veteran and father of three, [ 11 ] stole five children's videotapes from a K-Mart store in Ontario, California . Two weeks later, he stole four children's videotapes from a different K-Mart store in Montclair, California .

claims.claim: Andrade was sentenced to two consecutive terms of 25 years to life (fifty to life).
claims.episode_span: the same statute produced a fifty-to-life term for Leandro Andrade after he shoplifted nine videotapes
claims.supporting_quote: As a result of his prior convictions, Andrade was sentenced to two consecutive terms of 25 years to life in prison.

claims.claim: In Lockyer v. Andrade (2003) the U.S. Supreme Court held there was no habeas relief for the claim that Andrade's three-strikes sentence violated the Eighth Amendment, leaving the sentence standing.
claims.episode_span: Andrade’s sentence was upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court in 2003
claims.supporting_quote: held that there would be no relief by means of a petition for a writ of habeas corpus for a claim that a sentence imposed under California's three strikes law was an unconstitutionally disproportionate punishment prohibited by the Eighth Amendment's prohibition of cruel and unusual punishments .

claims.claim: The first three-strikes law was passed in 1993, when Washington voters approved Initiative 593.
claims.episode_span: The modern three-strikes movement began in Washington state in 1993 with Initiative 593, drafted after the murder of Diane Ballasiotes by a repeat offender on work release
claims.supporting_quote: The first true "three-strikes" law was passed in 1993, when Washington voters approved Initiative 593 .

claims.claim: California voters passed Proposition 184 in 1994 with 72% in favor.
claims.episode_span: California’s passed with 72 percent of the vote in November 1994 and applied retroactively to existing felony convictions
claims.supporting_quote: California passed its own in 1994, when their voters passed Proposition 184 [ 16 ] by an overwhelming majority, with 72% in favor and 28% against.

claims.claim: California's three-strikes act was signed into law on March 8, 1994, in the wake of the murder of Polly Klaas; Richard Allen Davis was convicted of her murder.
claims.episode_span: placed on the ballot after the abduction and killing of twelve-year-old Polly Klaas by Richard Allen Davis, who had an extensive prior record
claims.supporting_quote: In the wake of the murder, politicians in California and other U.S. states supported three strikes laws and California's Three Strikes act was signed into law on March 8, 1994.

claims.claim: Before the 2012 reform, a third strike meant a minimum of 25 years to life in California no matter what the third crime was.
claims.episode_span: the third — the one that triggered 25 years to life — could be any felony at all
claims.supporting_quote: Before 2012, the 3rd strike resulted in a minimum of 25 years to life imprisonment , no matter the 3rd crime in California

claims.claim: Proposition 36 passed on November 6, 2012 with 69.3% voting yes, and narrowed third strikes to serious or violent felonies.
claims.episode_span: produced Proposition 36, which voters approved in November 2012 by a 69 percent margin. The measure narrowed third-strike eligibility to serious or violent felonies and allowed resentencing for some inmates already serving life terms
claims.supporting_quote: The proposition was passed on November 6, 2012, with 8,575,619 people (69.3%) voting Yes and 3,798,218 people (30.7%) voting No.
